claim: CpG dinucleotides are the main mutational hot-spot in most cancers.
source: CpG dinucleotides are the main mutational hot-spot in most cancers.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without specific data from this study, drawing on general cancer genomics knowledge.

claim: The characteristic elevated C>T mutation rate in CpG sites has been related to 5-methylcytosine (5mC).
source: The characteristic elevated C>T mutation rate in CpG sites has been related to 5-methylcytosine (5mC), an epigenetically modified base which resides in CpGs and plays a role in transcription silencing.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about the relationship between 5mC and elevated C>T mutation rates.

claim: 5-methylcytosine is an epigenetically modified base which resides in CpGs and plays a role in transcription silencing.
source: The characteristic elevated C>T mutation rate in CpG sites has been related to 5-methylcytosine (5mC), an epigenetically modified base which resides in CpGs and plays a role in transcription silencing.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the properties and function of 5mC.

claim: In brain nearly a third of 5mCs have recently been found to exist in the form of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC).
source: In brain nearly a third of 5mCs have recently been found to exist in the form of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), yet the effect of 5hmC on mutational processes is still poorly understood.
evidence: This statement cites recent findings about 5hmC abundance in brain tissue, implicitly referencing prior literature.

claim: 5hmC is associated with an up to 53% decrease in the frequency of C>T mutations in a CpG context compared to 5mC.
source: Here we show that 5hmC is associated with an up to 53% decrease in the frequency of C>T mutations in a CpG context compared to 5mC.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tissue specific 5hmC patterns in brain, kidney and blood correlate with lower regional CpG>T mutation frequency in cancers originating in the respective tissues.
source: Tissue specific 5hmC patterns in brain, kidney and blood correlate with lower regional CpG>T mutation frequency in cancers originating in the respective tissues.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data analysis across multiple tissue types.

claim: The two most common cytosine modifications have global and opposing effects on the frequency of cancer causing somatic mutations in different cell types.
source: Together our data reveal global and opposing effects of the two most common cytosine modifications on the frequency of cancer causing somatic mutations in different cell types.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: The distribution of somatic mutations across the genome is not uniform.
source: Cancer genomics projects have revealed that the distribution of somatic mutations across the genome is not uniform (Lawrence et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lawrence et al., 2013.

claim: Chromatin organisation can influence regional mutation frequencies.
source: Apart from positive and negative selective pressure, a number of factors can influence regional mutation frequencies, such as chromatin organisation (Schuster-Böckler and Lehner, 2012), replication timing (Koren et al., 2012), metabolic load (Ames et al., 1993) and exposure to different mutagens (Poon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schuster-Böckler and Lehner, 2012.

claim: Replication timing can influence regional mutation frequencies.
source: Apart from positive and negative selective pressure, a number of factors can influence regional mutation frequencies, such as chromatin organisation (Schuster-Böckler and Lehner, 2012), replication timing (Koren et al., 2012), metabolic load (Ames et al., 1993) and exposure to different mutagens (Poon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koren et al., 2012.

claim: Metabolic load can influence regional mutation frequencies.
source: Apart from positive and negative selective pressure, a number of factors can influence regional mutation frequencies, such as chromatin organisation (Schuster-Böckler and Lehner, 2012), replication timing (Koren et al., 2012), metabolic load (Ames et al., 1993) and exposure to different mutagens (Poon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ames et al., 1993.

claim: Exposure to different mutagens can influence regional mutation frequencies.
source: Apart from positive and negative selective pressure, a number of factors can influence regional mutation frequencies, such as chromatin organisation (Schuster-Böckler and Lehner, 2012), replication timing (Koren et al., 2012), metabolic load (Ames et al., 1993) and exposure to different mutagens (Poon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poon et al., 2013.

claim: Highly transcribed regions generally exhibit lower mutation frequencies due to the influence of transcription-coupled repair.
source: Furthermore, highly transcribed regions generally exhibit lower mutation frequencies due to the influence of transcription-coupled repair (Lawrence et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lawrence et al., 2013.

claim: Consensus motifs for cytidine deaminases (such as APOBEC and AID) were found enriched at mutational hot-spots.
source: For example, consensus motifs for cytidine deaminases (such as APOBEC and AID) were found enriched at mutational hot-spots, suggesting that activity of these enzymes could be the potential cause of those mutations (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nik-Zainal et al., 2012 and Taylor et al., 2013.

claim: Activity of cytidine deaminases could be the potential cause of mutations at hot-spots.
source: For example, consensus motifs for cytidine deaminases (such as APOBEC and AID) were found enriched at mutational hot-spots, suggesting that activity of these enzymes could be the potential cause of those mutations (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the enrichment of motifs, supported by citations.

claim: The most frequent mutational signature found in the majority of cancers is C to T transition in a CpG dinucleotide context (CpG>T).
source: The most frequent mutational signature found in the majority of cancers is C to T transition in a CpG dinucleotide context (CpG>T) (Alexandrov et al., 2013; Lawrence et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alexandrov et al., 2013 and Lawrence et al., 2013.

claim: Cytosines in CpG dinucleotides are frequently methylated to form 5-methylcytosine (5mC).
source: This relates to the fact that cytosines in CpG dinucleotides are frequently methylated to form 5-methylcytosine (5mC).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DNA methylation.

claim: The rate of spontaneous deamination of 5mC into T is four fold higher than the rate of deamination of C into U.
source: The rate of spontaneous deamination of 5mC into T is four fold higher than the rate of deamination of C into U (Lindahl and Nyberg, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lindahl and Nyberg, 1974.

claim: In the germline of vertebrates, elevated deamination of 5mC likely facilitated a general depletion of CpGs outside of CpG islands which are largely unmethylated.
source: In the germline of vertebrates, this likely facilitated a general depletion of CpGs outside of CpG islands which are largely unmethylated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the higher deamination rate of 5mC and evolutionary patterns.

claim: The genomes of all examined vertebrate species feature DNA methylation.
source: The genomes of all examined vertebrate species feature DNA methylation, and loss of DNA methylation is incompatible with normal development in mice (Li et al., 1992; Okano et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about vertebrate genomes.

claim: Loss of DNA methylation is incompatible with normal development in mice.
source: The genomes of all examined vertebrate species feature DNA methylation, and loss of DNA methylation is incompatible with normal development in mice (Li et al., 1992; Okano et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 1992 and Okano et al., 1999.

claim: DNA methylation plays a role in gene expression, most notably by repressing one allele of imprinted genes.
source: DNA methylation plays a role in gene expression, most notably by repressing one allele of imprinted genes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DNA methylation function.

claim: DNA methylation is involved in maintenance of genome stability, alternative splicing, X chromosome inactivation and suppression of retrotransposons.
source: Moreover, it is involved in maintenance of genome stability, alternative splicing, X chromosome inactivation and suppression of retrotransposons (Klose and Bird, 2006; Jones, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Klose and Bird, 2006 and Jones, 2012.

claim: In 2009, 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) was indisputably shown to exist in DNA of brain and other tissues.
source: In 2009, 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) was indisputably shown to exist in DNA of brain and other tissues (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009.

claim: Ten-eleven translocation (TET) enzymes are able to convert 5mC into 5hmC.
source: It was concurrently shown that ten-eleven translocation (TET) enzymes are able to convert 5mC into 5hmC (Tahiliani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tahiliani et al., 2009.

claim: Unlike 5mC, which is observed at similar levels in many cell types, the abundance of 5hmC varies widely.
source: Unlike 5mC, which is observed at similar levels in many cell types, the abundance of 5hmC varies widely.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the differential distribution of these modifications.

claim: 5hmC was observed to be particularly enriched in brain cells.
source: 5hmC was observed to be particularly enriched in brain cells (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009; Lister et al., 2013) and detectable in embryonic stem cells and all examined tissues (Tahiliani et al., 2009; Globisch et al., 2010; Szwagierczak et al., 2010; Wu and Zhang, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009 and Lister et al., 2013.

claim: 5hmC is detectable in embryonic stem cells and all examined tissues.
source: 5hmC was observed to be particularly enriched in brain cells (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009; Lister et al., 2013) and detectable in embryonic stem cells and all examined tissues (Tahiliani et al., 2009; Globisch et al., 2010; Szwagierczak et al., 2010; Wu and Zhang, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tahiliani et al., 2009; Globisch et al., 2010; Szwagierczak et al., 2010; Wu and Zhang, 2011.

claim: 5hmC and higher oxidised states of methyl-cytosine have been proposed to play a role in de-methylation via ineffective re-methylation after replication or directly by thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG).
source: 5hmC and higher oxidised states of methyl-cytosine have been proposed to play a role in de-methylation via ineffective re-methylation after replication or directly by thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG) (Tahiliani et al., 2009; He et al., 2011; Maiti and Drohat, 2011; Shen et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies proposing this mechanism.

claim: 5hmC has been implicated in transcriptional regulation.
source: In addition to demethylation, 5hmC has been implicated in transcriptional regulation, and a number of DNA binding proteins recognising 5hmC have been identified (Mellén et al., 2012; Spruijt et al., 2013; Takai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mellén et al., 2012; Spruijt et al., 2013; Takai et al., 2014.

claim: A number of DNA binding proteins recognising 5hmC have been identified.
source: In addition to demethylation, 5hmC has been implicated in transcriptional regulation, and a number of DNA binding proteins recognising 5hmC have been identified (Mellén et al., 2012; Spruijt et al., 2013; Takai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mellén et al., 2012; Spruijt et al., 2013; Takai et al., 2014.

claim: 5hmC is found depleted in primary tumours.
source: 5hmC is found depleted in primary tumours and TET2 is frequently mutated in myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myelogenous leukaemia and T-cell lymphoma, indicating that 5hmC plays a role in carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about 5hmC levels in tumors.

claim: TET2 is frequently mutated in myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myelogenous leukaemia and T-cell lymphoma.
source: 5hmC is found depleted in primary tumours and TET2 is frequently mutated in myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myelogenous leukaemia and T-cell lymphoma, indicating that 5hmC plays a role in carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about TET2 mutations in specific cancers.

claim: 5hmC plays a role in carcinogenesis.
source: 5hmC is found depleted in primary tumours and TET2 is frequently mutated in myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myelogenous leukaemia and T-cell lymphoma, indicating that 5hmC plays a role in carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the depletion of 5hmC in tumors and TET2 mutations.

claim: The molecular mechanism by which 5hmC affects carcinogenesis is poorly understood.
source: However, the molecular mechanism by which 5hmC affects carcinogenesis is poorly understood (Rasmussen and Helin, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rasmussen and Helin, 2016.

claim: 5hmC is an important intermediate during demethylation in zygotes and ES cells.
source: 5hmC is an important intermediate during demethylation in zygotes and ES cells (Tahiliani et al., 2009; Inoue and Zhang, 2011; Wossidlo et al., 2011), but the vast majority of 5hmC is found as a stable, long-lived modification in adult mouse tissue that undergoes little cell division (Bachman et al., 2014; Brazauskas and Kriaucionis, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tahiliani et al., 2009; Inoue and Zhang, 2011; Wossidlo et al., 2011.

claim: The vast majority of 5hmC is found as a stable, long-lived modification in adult mouse tissue that undergoes little cell division.
source: 5hmC is an important intermediate during demethylation in zygotes and ES cells (Tahiliani et al., 2009; Inoue and Zhang, 2011; Wossidlo et al., 2011), but the vast majority of 5hmC is found as a stable, long-lived modification in adult mouse tissue that undergoes little cell division (Bachman et al., 2014; Brazauskas and Kriaucionis, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bachman et al., 2014 and Brazauskas and Kriaucionis, 2014.

claim: Long-lived 5hmC could have a substantial influence on the mutability of DNA.
source: Thus, we hypothesised that – similar to 5mC – long-lived 5hmC could have a substantial influence on the mutability of DNA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the stability of 5hmC.

claim: Supek et al. reported elevated C>G transversion rates at 5hmC sites, using 5hmC maps from human and mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: Recently, Supek et al. (Supek et al., 2014) reported elevated C>G transversion rates at 5hmC sites, using 5hmC maps from human and mouse embryonic stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Supek et al., 2014.

claim: Embryonic stem cells differ substantially from the somatic tissues in which mutations were observed.
source: However, these findings are limited by the fact that embryonic stem cells differ substantially from the somatic tissues in which mutations were observed (Schultz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schultz et al., 2015.

claim: A large proportion of mutations observed in any cancer genome originate in its pre-cancerous cell of origin.
source: A large proportion of mutations observed in any cancer genome originate in its pre-cancerous cell of origin (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2012; Tomasetti et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2015) and will have been influenced by its epigenetic landscape.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2012; Tomasetti et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2015.

claim: Mutations in cancer genomes will have been influenced by the epigenetic landscape of the pre-cancerous cell of origin.
source: A large proportion of mutations observed in any cancer genome originate in its pre-cancerous cell of origin (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2012; Tomasetti et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2015) and will have been influenced by its epigenetic landscape.
evidence: This is an inference based on the origin of mutations in pre-cancerous cells.

claim: 5hmC has been shown to be most abundant in human brain.
source: Since 5hmC has been shown to be most abundant in human brain (Li and Liu, 2011; Nestor et al., 2012), we have initially focussed on assessing the relationship between mutability and DNA modifications in brain cancers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li and Liu, 2011 and Nestor et al., 2012.

claim: The dominant mutational signature in brain cancers is CpG>T.
source: Based on a DNA sequencing data from five brain cancer types encompassing 665 patients, we show that the dominant mutational signature in brain cancers is CpG>T, which is modulated by the modification state of cytosine.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of brain cancer sequencing data.

claim: The CpG>T mutational signature in brain cancers is modulated by the modification state of cytosine.
source: Based on a DNA sequencing data from five brain cancer types encompassing 665 patients, we show that the dominant mutational signature in brain cancers is CpG>T, which is modulated by the modification state of cytosine.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The CpG>T mutation frequency of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine is reduced nearly two-fold compared to the methylated state.
source: Strikingly, the CpG>T mutation frequency of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine is reduced nearly two-fold compared to the methylated state.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The ratio of 5hmC to 5mC in 100 kb genomic intervals correlates with CpG>T mutation frequency even after accounting for confounding factors like gene density or CpG islands.
source: We find that the ratio of 5hmC to 5mC in 100 kb genomic intervals correlates with CpG>T mutation frequency even after accounting for confounding factors like gene density or CpG islands.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's statistical analysis.

claim: A clear tissue-specific effect of 5hmC on mutagenicity is observed in kidney and myeloid lineage of blood cells.
source: When we expand our analysis to include mutations and 5hmC maps from kidney and myeloid lineage of blood cells, we observe a clear tissue-specific effect of 5hmC on mutagenicity.
evidence: This is a finding from the expanded analysis across multiple tissues.

claim: Reduced 5hmC levels associate with an increased proportion of CpG>T mutations in cancers of the corresponding tissue.
source: Finally, we measured 5mC and 5hmC levels using methodology of high accuracy in eight different human tissue types and show that reduced 5hmC levels associate with an increased proportion of CpG>T mutations in cancers of the corresponding tissue.
evidence: This is a finding from HPLC measurements and correlation analysis.

claim: Hydroxymethylation has a significant influence on the likelihood of mutations at CpG sites across many human tissue types.
source: Together, our findings suggest that hydroxymethylation has a significant influence on the likelihood of mutations at CpG sites across many human tissue types.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings across multiple tissues.

claim: 5hmC predominantly occurs in a CpG context.
source: As 5hmC predominantly occurs in a CpG context, we focussed the analysis on CpG sites.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation about 5hmC distribution.

claim: Brain tissue exhibits particularly high levels of 5hmC.
source: Since brain tissue has been shown to exhibit particularly high levels of 5hmC (Figure 1A), we first investigated the relationship between the regional distribution of 5hmC, 5mC and mutagenesis in brain tumours.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing 5hmC distribution data.

claim: 5hmC levels are visibly and significantly anti-correlated with the frequency of CpG>T mutations.
source: Strikingly, 5hmC levels were visibly and significantly anti-correlated with the frequency of CpG>T (r=-0.71, chr3), while 5mC levels displayed a positive correlation (r=0.66, chr3, Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and visualization in figures.

claim: 5mC levels display a positive correlation with the frequency of CpG>T mutations.
source: Strikingly, 5hmC levels were visibly and significantly anti-correlated with the frequency of CpG>T (r=-0.71, chr3), while 5mC levels displayed a positive correlation (r=0.66, chr3, Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and visualization in figures.

claim: The fraction of mutated 5hmChigh sites was significantly lower than the fraction of mutated 5mChigh sites.
source: The fraction of mutated 5hmChigh sites was significantly lower than the fraction of mutated 5mChigh sites (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The lower mutation frequency at 5hmC sites was consistently observed in data derived from both exome and whole genome sequencing projects.
source: The lower mutation frequency was consistently observed in data derived from both exome and whole genome sequencing projects (p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of both types of sequencing data.

claim: All brain cancer types individually displayed a significant (28–53%, p<0.05 in all types) reduction of C>T mutations in 5hmChigh sites.
source: Moreover, all brain cancer types individually displayed a significant (28–53%, p<0.05 in all types) reduction of C>T mutations in 5hmChigh sites (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis across all brain cancer types shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: CpG>T mutations are one of the two mutational signatures correlating with age.
source: It has been shown that CpG>T mutations are one of the two mutational signatures correlating with age (Alexandrov et al., 2015), supporting the fact that these mutations were gathered during the entire lives of the patients, not only after the origin of cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alexandrov et al., 2015.

claim: CpG>T mutations were gathered during the entire lives of the patients, not only after the origin of cancer.
source: It has been shown that CpG>T mutations are one of the two mutational signatures correlating with age (Alexandrov et al., 2015), supporting the fact that these mutations were gathered during the entire lives of the patients, not only after the origin of cancer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the age correlation of CpG>T mutations.

claim: The correlation between CpG>T mutations and age is present in both methylated and hydroxymethylated sites.
source: Here we observed that this correlation is present in both methylated and hydroxymethylated sites (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The slope for 5mC age correlation was steeper than for 5hmC.
source: Moreover, the slope for 5mC was steeper than for 5hmC, suggesting that even the mechanisms causing the difference of CpG>T mutability between 5mC and 5hmC were present in the pre-cancerous cell of origin.
evidence: This is an observation from the age correlation analysis.

claim: The mechanisms causing the difference of CpG>T mutability between 5mC and 5hmC were present in the pre-cancerous cell of origin.
source: Moreover, the slope for 5mC was steeper than for 5hmC, suggesting that even the mechanisms causing the difference of CpG>T mutability between 5mC and 5hmC were present in the pre-cancerous cell of origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential slopes of age correlation.

claim: C>A or C>G transversions are an order of magnitude less frequent than C>T transitions in both 5mC and 5hmC sites.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, C>A or C>G transversions are an order of magnitude less frequent than C>T transitions in both 5mC and 5hmC sites.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In GBM and LGG the frequency of C>A mutations was significantly higher in 5mChigh compared to 5hmChigh sites.
source: In GBM and LGG the frequency of C>A mutations was significantly higher in 5mChigh compared to 5hmChigh sites, but in NRB, MDB and PA we detected no significant difference.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of C>A mutations across cancer types.

claim: In NRB, MDB and PA there was no significant difference in C>A mutation frequency between 5mChigh and 5hmChigh sites.
source: In GBM and LGG the frequency of C>A mutations was significantly higher in 5mChigh compared to 5hmChigh sites, but in NRB, MDB and PA we detected no significant difference.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The frequency of C>G mutations in 5mChigh sites differed significantly from 5hmChigh sites only in MDB, PA and GBM.
source: The frequency of C>G mutations in 5mChigh sites differed significantly from 5hmChigh sites only in MDB, PA and GBM.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of C>G mutations.

claim: In MDB and PA, 5hmChigh sites were slightly enriched for C>G mutations.
source: In MDB and PA, 5hmChigh sites were slightly enriched for C>G mutations, whereas in GBM an enrichment was observed at 5mChigh sites.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: In GBM an enrichment of C>G mutations was observed at 5mChigh sites.
source: In MDB and PA, 5hmChigh sites were slightly enriched for C>G mutations, whereas in GBM an enrichment was observed at 5mChigh sites.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: C>T transitions are the most common somatic mutation type in brain.
source: Since C>T transitions are the most common somatic mutation type in brain and the difference in C>T mutations between 5mChigh and 5hmChigh sites is more consistent among cancer types than in the C>A and C>G transversions, we focus mainly on C>T mutations in the remainder of this report.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The difference in C>T mutations between 5mChigh and 5hmChigh sites is more consistent among cancer types than in the C>A and C>G transversions.
source: Since C>T transitions are the most common somatic mutation type in brain and the difference in C>T mutations between 5mChigh and 5hmChigh sites is more consistent among cancer types than in the C>A and C>G transversions, we focus mainly on C>T mutations in the remainder of this report.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing mutation patterns across cancer types.

claim: C>T mutations are significantly depleted at 5hmC sites across a wide range of thresholds in definitions of 5mChigh and 5hmChigh.
source: We confirmed that C>T mutations are significantly depleted at 5hmC sites across a wide range of thresholds in definitions of 5mChigh and 5hmChigh (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: More stringent definitions of 5hmC result in even greater differences (42–59%) in C>T mutation frequencies between 5mChigh and 5hmChigh sites.
source: In fact, more stringent definitions of 5hmC (e.g., 5hmChigh: 5hmC level / mod level ≥ 0.7) result in even greater differences (42–59%) in C>T mutation frequencies between 5mChigh and 5hmChigh sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D), but these definitions would reduce the number of sites too much for our subsequent statistical analyses.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: 5hmC density is elevated in highly expressed genes in brain.
source: For example, 5hmC density is elevated in highly expressed genes in brain (Mellén et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012; Lister et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: There was a lower overall mutation frequency in highly expressed genes.
source: There was a lower overall mutation frequency in highly expressed genes (Figure 3A–B), but both highly and lowly expressed genes exhibited significantly lower C>T transition rates at 5hmC sites compared to 5mC sites (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A–B.

claim: Both highly and lowly expressed genes exhibited significantly lower C>T transition rates at 5hmC sites compared to 5mC sites.
source: There was a lower overall mutation frequency in highly expressed genes (Figure 3A–B), but both highly and lowly expressed genes exhibited significantly lower C>T transition rates at 5hmC sites compared to 5mC sites (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: The observed effect of 5hmC on mutation frequency is independent of transcription and thus not a result of transcription coupled repair.
source: This suggests that the observed effect is independent of transcription and thus not a result of transcription coupled repair.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the effect persists in both highly and lowly expressed genes.

claim: The frequency of C>T mutations in 5hmC remained significantly lower than in 5mC in the paired analysis.
source: Nevertheless, the frequency of C>T mutations in 5hmC remained significantly lower than in 5mC in both exomes and genomes (Figure 3E–F), supporting that the difference between 5mC and 5hmC mutation frequency is not caused by regional differences.
evidence: This is supported by data from the paired analysis shown in Figure 3E–F.

claim: The difference between 5mC and 5hmC mutation frequency is not caused by regional differences.
source: Nevertheless, the frequency of C>T mutations in 5hmC remained significantly lower than in 5mC in both exomes and genomes (Figure 3E–F), supporting that the difference between 5mC and 5hmC mutation frequency is not caused by regional differences.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the paired analysis controlling for regional effects.

claim: The mutation frequency differed substantially in the aligned positions of DNA modifications but was indistinguishable in the surrounding area.
source: The mutation frequency differed substantially in the aligned positions of DNA modifications but was indistinguishable in the surrounding area.
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial analysis of mutations around modified sites.

claim: Regional mutation rate variability is unlikely to account for the difference in C>T mutational load in 5mC and 5hmC sites.
source: In conclusion, regional mutation rate variability is unlikely to account for the difference in C>T mutational load in 5mC and 5hmC sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence controlling for regional effects.

claim: There is a clear linear relationship between 5hmCrel values and C>T mutation frequencies.
source: We observed a clear linear relationship between 5hmCrel values and C>T mutation frequencies.
evidence: This is an observation from the binned analysis of 5hmCrel and mutation frequency.

claim: The correlation between 5hmCrel and C>T mutation frequency was present in all the tested brain cancer types in exome- and whole genome-sequenced samples.
source: Notably, the correlation was present in all the tested brain cancer types in exome- and whole genome-sequenced samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis across all brain cancer types.

claim: A regression slope test confirmed significance of the relationship between 5hmCrel and C>T mutation frequency in all the cancer types.
source: A regression slope test confirmed significance of this relationship in all the cancer types.
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the regression analysis.

claim: An increase in 5hmCrel is associated with an increase in C>G mutations in whole genomes from MDB and PA samples.
source: Consistent with our previous results, an increase in 5hmCrel is associated with an increase in C>G mutations in whole genomes (from MDB and PA samples), but the relationship in other cancer types shows no significant trend.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of C>G mutations.

claim: C>A mutations decrease with 5hmCrel levels in GBM but exhibit no significant signal in the remaining tumour types.
source: C>A mutations decrease with 5hmCrel levels in GBM but exhibit no significant signal in the remaining tumour types.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of C>A mutations.

claim: The mutation frequency of unmodified cytosine is similar to 5hmC.
source: We observed that the mutation frequency of unmodified cytosine is similar to 5hmC, whereas 5mC exhibited much higher mutation frequency (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 5mC exhibited much higher mutation frequency than unmodified cytosine and 5hmC.
source: We observed that the mutation frequency of unmodified cytosine is similar to 5hmC, whereas 5mC exhibited much higher mutation frequency (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When methylated sites are excluded, the mutation frequency does not show any significant trend with increasing levels of 5hmC.
source: When methylated sites are excluded, the mutation frequency does not show any significant trend with increasing levels of 5hmC (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Excluding hydroxymethylated sites leads to a significant gradient in mutation frequency with increasing levels of 5mC.
source: Conversely, excluding hydroxymethylated sites leads to a significant gradient in mutation frequency with increasing levels of 5mC (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: When only fully modified sites are taken into account, increasing levels of 5hmC are associated with a significant decrease in C>T mutation frequency.
source: When only fully modified sites (mod level ≥ 90%) are taken into account, increasing levels of 5hmC (i.e., decreasing levels of 5mC) are associated with a significant decrease in C>T mutation frequency (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The best individual predictor of CpG>T mutation frequency was 5hmCrel.
source: The best individual predictor of CpG>T mutation frequency was 5hmCrel (D2 = 0.11), outperforming all other features (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the GLM analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Bisulfite sequencing measurements alone are a poor predictor of mutagenicity.
source: Interestingly, the sum of 5mC and 5hmC levels ('mod') performed worst, suggesting that bisulfite sequencing measurements alone are a poor predictor of mutagenicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the poor performance of 'mod' in the GLM analysis.

claim: When combining all 11 features into one model, the total explained deviance for 100 kb windows was 16%.
source: When combining all 11 features into one model, the total explained deviance for 100 kb windows was 16%.
evidence: This is a result from the multivariate GLM analysis.

claim: 5hmCrel significantly contributes to the deviance explained by the model, beyond covariation with gene expression.
source: In line with our earlier results, we found that 5hmCrel significantly contributes to the deviance explained by the model, beyond covariation with gene expression (Figure 5C–D; F-test p<2e-100).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: The unique contribution of 5hmCrel to the explained gene mutation frequency decreased as the mutation sets became larger and more distant from modC>T.
source: Indeed, the unique contribution of 5hmCrel to the explained gene mutation frequency decreased as the mutation sets became larger and more distant from modC>T (Figure 5C–D, Figure 5—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: 5hmCrel had no significant predictive power for the frequency of T>N mutations.
source: Conversely, we confirmed that 5hmCrel had no significant predictive power for the frequency of T>N mutations (Figure 5C–D; column T>N), supporting the hypothesis that 5hmCrel selectively affects mutations in modified cytosines.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: 5hmCrel selectively affects mutations in modified cytosines.
source: Conversely, we confirmed that 5hmCrel had no significant predictive power for the frequency of T>N mutations (Figure 5C–D; column T>N), supporting the hypothesis that 5hmCrel selectively affects mutations in modified cytosines.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect on T>N mutations.

claim: 5hmC sites in kidney were mutated significantly less frequently than 5mC sites.
source: Matching our findings in brain, 5hmC sites were mutated significantly less frequently than 5mC sites in both tissue types (Figure 6B), irrespective of whether genome or exome sequencing data were used.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B for kidney.

claim: 5hmC sites in blood were mutated significantly less frequently than 5mC sites.
source: Matching our findings in brain, 5hmC sites were mutated significantly less frequently than 5mC sites in both tissue types (Figure 6B), irrespective of whether genome or exome sequencing data were used.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B for blood.

claim: For each cancer type, the best predictor of CpG>T mutation rate came from the same tissue type.
source: Strikingly, for each cancer type, the best predictor came from the same tissue type (Figure 6A), suggesting that tissue differences in 5hmC are reflected in the CpG>T mutation landscape.
evidence: This is supported by the GLM analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Tissue differences in 5hmC are reflected in the CpG>T mutation landscape.
source: Strikingly, for each cancer type, the best predictor came from the same tissue type (Figure 6A), suggesting that tissue differences in 5hmC are reflected in the CpG>T mutation landscape.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tissue-specific predictive power of 5hmC maps.

claim: The ESC-derived 5hmC levels have substantially lower predictive power on CpG>T mutation rate than any of the tissue-derived maps.
source: As we anticipated, the ESC-derived 5hmC levels have substantially lower predictive power on CpG>T mutation rate than any of the tissue-derived maps.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative GLM analysis.

claim: Tissues with high levels of 5hmC relative to 5mC would exhibit fewer CpG>T mutations in modified sites than tissues with low total 5hmC.
source: Given our findings thus far, we predicted that tissues with high levels of 5hmC relative to 5mC would exhibit fewer CpG>T mutations in modified sites than tissues with low total 5hmC.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the study's findings.

claim: There is a strong negative correlation between genomic 5hmC and enrichment of CpG>T mutations in all tissue types except lung.
source: The analysis of association between genomic 5hmC and enrichment of CpG>T mutations revealed a strong negative correlation (Figure 6C) in all tissue types except lung.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The difference in lung cancer seems to stem from smoking-related effects.
source: Interestingly, this difference seems to stem from smoking-related effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of smoking-related mutation patterns.

claim: Lung cancer mutation data from heavy smokers revealed a markedly lower frequency of CpG>T mutations in modified sites, relative to other mutations.
source: Lung cancer mutation data from heavy smokers revealed a markedly lower frequency of CpG>T mutations in modified sites, relative to other mutations.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of smoking-stratified lung cancer data.

claim: The typical C>A mutational signature associated with smoking was found significantly enriched in CpGs outside CpG islands.
source: It has been reported that the typical C>A mutational signature associated with smoking was found significantly enriched in CpGs outside CpG islands, suggesting that it preferentially occurs at modified CpG sites (Pleasance et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pleasance et al., 2010.

claim: Smoking-related C>A mutations preferentially occur at modified CpG sites.
source: It has been reported that the typical C>A mutational signature associated with smoking was found significantly enriched in CpGs outside CpG islands, suggesting that it preferentially occurs at modified CpG sites (Pleasance et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment pattern, supported by citation.

claim: CpG>T mutations might be differentially affected by smoking-related mutagens.
source: Accordingly, our data indicate that CpG>T mutations might also be differentially affected by smoking-related mutagens.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns in smoking-related lung cancers.

claim: 5hmCs carry between 28 and 53% fewer mutations than methylated cytosines in brain.
source: Our measurements indicate that 5hmCs carry between 28 and 53% fewer mutations than methylated cytosines in brain.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings in brain tissue.

claim: The mutational load at 5hmC sites is comparable to that of unmodified cytosines in CpG dinucleotides.
source: This results in a mutational load at 5hmC sites that is comparable to that of unmodified cytosines in CpG dinucleotides.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of mutation frequencies.

claim: The relationship between 5hmC and CpG>T mutation rate can be detected at the scale of the exome as well as genome-wide.
source: The relationship between 5hmC and CpG>T mutation rate can be detected at the scale of the exome as well as genome-wide and is independent of other region-specific influences on mutation frequency.
evidence: This is a summary of findings across different scales of analysis.

claim: The relationship between 5hmC and CpG>T mutation rate is independent of other region-specific influences on mutation frequency.
source: The relationship between 5hmC and CpG>T mutation rate can be detected at the scale of the exome as well as genome-wide and is independent of other region-specific influences on mutation frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the various control analyses performed.

claim: The relative impact of hydroxymethylation on mutagenesis decreases proportionally to the level of 5hmC in the tissue.
source: We show that the relative impact of hydroxymethylation on mutagenesis decreases proportionally to the level of 5hmC in the tissue, suggesting that it represents a general property of this DNA modification.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation analysis across tissues.

claim: The effect of 5hmC on mutagenesis represents a general property of this DNA modification.
source: We show that the relative impact of hydroxymethylation on mutagenesis decreases proportionally to the level of 5hmC in the tissue, suggesting that it represents a general property of this DNA modification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistent patterns observed across tissues.

claim: Spontaneous and enzymatic deamination reactions of 5hmC could be less favourable than 5mC.
source: Firstly, spontaneous and enzymatic deamination reactions of 5hmC could be less favourable than 5mC.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference in mutation rates.

claim: Cytosine deaminases (namely, AID and APOBEC1-3) have 4.4–38x lower activity on sites with 5hmC compared to 5mC.
source: Indeed, cytosine deaminases (namely, AID and APOBEC1-3) have 4.4–38x lower activity on sites with 5hmC compared to 5mC, supporting this possibility (Nabel et al., 2012; Rangam et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nabel et al., 2012 and Rangam et al., 2012.

claim: Deamination of 5mC produces thymine.
source: Secondly, deamination of 5mC produces thymine whereas 5hmC deaminates to 5-hydroxymethyluracil (5hmU).
evidence: This is stated as established biochemical knowledge.

claim: 5hmC deaminates to 5-hydroxymethyluracil (5hmU).
source: Secondly, deamination of 5mC produces thymine whereas 5hmC deaminates to 5-hydroxymethyluracil (5hmU).
evidence: This is stated as established biochemical knowledge.

claim: 5-hydroxymethyluracil could be more efficiently recognised and replaced by the DNA glycosylases initiating base-excision repair (BER).
source: This atypical base in DNA could be more efficiently recognised and replaced by the DNA glycosylases initiating base-excision repair (BER).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lower mutation rate at 5hmC sites.

claim: TDG and MBD4 excise both T and 5hmU when mis-paired with G.
source: TDG and MBD4 excise both T and 5hmU when mis-paired with G (Hardeland et al., 2003; Cortellino et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2011; Hashimoto et al., 2012; Moréra et al., 2012), whereas SMUG1 does not repair T:G but has a robust activity for 5hmU:G (Nilsen et al., 2001; Kemmerich et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on DNA glycosylase activities.

claim: SMUG1 does not repair T:G but has a robust activity for 5hmU:G.
source: TDG and MBD4 excise both T and 5hmU when mis-paired with G (Hardeland et al., 2003; Cortellino et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2011; Hashimoto et al., 2012; Moréra et al., 2012), whereas SMUG1 does not repair T:G but has a robust activity for 5hmU:G (Nilsen et al., 2001; Kemmerich et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nilsen et al., 2001 and Kemmerich et al., 2012.

claim: There might be more efficient repair of 5hmU in the genome.
source: Therefore, there might be more efficient repair of 5hmU in the genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential activities of DNA glycosylases.

claim: Supek et al. observed only a very small (albeit statistically significant) decrease of C>T mutations in 5hmC sites in both SNPs and cancer SNVs.
source: As part of this analysis, only a very small (albeit statistically significant) decrease of C>T mutations in 5hmC sites in both SNPs and cancer SNVs was observed.
evidence: This is a reference to findings from Supek et al.'s study.

claim: Supek et al. consider all sites with as little as one 5hmC read to be hydroxymethylated.
source: Firstly, Supek et al. consider all sites with as little as one 5hmC read to be hydroxymethylated, whereas we require the level of 5hmC to exceed 5mC.
evidence: This is a description of methodological differences between studies.

claim: 5hmC genomic localisation in embryonic stem cells was a poor predictor of CpG>T mutations in brain, kidney and blood, compared to the respective tissue-specific 5hmC patterns.
source: Specifically, 5hmC genomic localisation in embryonic stem cells was a poor predictor of CpG>T mutations in brain, kidney and blood, compared to the respective tissue-specific 5hmC patterns.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of ESC vs tissue-specific 5hmC maps.

claim: The slow accumulation of CpG>T mutations in the pre-cancerous tissue was strongly influenced by the DNA modification landscape.
source: This provides evidence that the slow accumulation of CpG>T mutations in the pre-cancerous tissue was strongly influenced by the DNA modification landscape.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tissue-specific predictive power of 5hmC maps.

claim: Solid tumours originate from a defined subset of cells within any one tissue type.
source: Mounting evidence suggests that solid tumours originate from a defined subset of cells within any one tissue type.
evidence: This is stated as an emerging understanding in cancer biology.

claim: Glioblastomas were proposed to originate from stem or progenitor cell types enriched in the subventricular zone.
source: For example, glioblastomas were proposed to originate from stem or progenitor cell types enriched in the subventricular zone, while medulloblastomas have mixed cells of origin (Visvader, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Visvader, 2011.

claim: Medulloblastomas have mixed cells of origin.
source: For example, glioblastomas were proposed to originate from stem or progenitor cell types enriched in the subventricular zone, while medulloblastomas have mixed cells of origin (Visvader, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Visvader, 2011.

claim: The DNA modification landscape in cancer-progenitor cells is sufficiently similar to the tissue average to be informative about the mutation frequencies in cancer.
source: The fact that we observe a clear inverse relationship between CpG>T mutations and the location of 5hmC in multiple tissue types suggests that the DNA modification landscape in cancer-progenitor cells is sufficiently similar to the tissue average to be informative about the mutation frequencies in cancer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlations despite tissue heterogeneity.

claim: The impact of DNA modifications on the frequency of CpG>T mutations is likely to be bigger than measured in this study.
source: Under this assumption we predict that the impact of DNA modifications on the frequency of CpG>T mutations is likely to be bigger than measured here, since the terminally differentiated cells that make up the bulk of the tissue may have diverged further from cancer-progenitor cells.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the assumption about tissue heterogeneity.

claim: The strong correlation between relative 5hmC levels in a tissue and the mutability of modified cytosine points towards a shared underlying mutagenic process.
source: The strong correlation between relative 5hmC levels in a tissue and the mutability of modified cytosine also points towards a shared underlying mutagenic process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistent correlation across tissues.

claim: A yet undefined smoking-induced mutagenic mechanism preferentially affects unmethylated CpG sites.
source: We speculate that a yet undefined smoking-induced mutagenic mechanism preferentially affects unmethylated CpG sites.
evidence: This is speculation based on the deviation observed in smoking-related lung cancers.

claim: The linear relationship between 5hmC levels and CpG>T mutation rate could be used to identify other environmental mutagens with a differential effect on modified cytosines.
source: In the future, the linear relationship between 5hmC levels and CpG>T mutation rate could thus be used to identify other environmental mutagens with a differential effect on modified cytosines.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the findings.
